deck_zh: 修正案通过了。可让人追问它的选举、续期和审查，也一起被它改动了。
deck_en: The amendment passed. It also changed the elections, renewal procedures, and review through which people could challenge its authors.
body_zh: 反对方的广告没有按原样播出。广告提到了军队部署，送审之后，被要求删改。同一场公投里，边境三个区没有设投票站，约两万六千名登记选民没能投票。入秋，结果公布：投票率百分之四十一点二，赞成票百分之五十八点三。第十四修正案生效。
继续看那三个条款，才知道这场投票改动了什么。战时不选举，战时状态结束后六个月内再选，议员和首席执政的任期跟着延长；紧急状态可以由执政院自行续期，每次最长一百八十天，议会要五分之三才能终止；法院要宣布紧急令不合宪章，十一位法官中得有八位同意。
这是目的联合城邦的假想故事。提出修正案的是执政院，提出时，紧急状态才宣布十二天。法律事务局的附件解释得很清楚：现行紧急状态法不许用紧急令推迟选举，要推迟，只能修宪。它没有违反这条禁令。它找到了一条能改动禁令背后安排的路。
难处也在这里。不是首席执政一个人签字就改了宪章。两院都表决了，公投也举行了，每一个步骤都在原有修正程序里。问题不是“有没有手续”，而是走完手续之后，还有什么不能只拿手续来回答。
我们很容易把三个不同的问题压成一句“合法不合法”。第一，它有没有实际作用？有。选举因此延期，紧急权力因此继续。第二，它有没有按当时的权限和程序生效？在这份案卷里，有。第三，让它这样作用在人身上，究竟凭什么？前两问答完，第三问才刚开始。
## 祖先的签名没有替今天的人签完
联合城邦的宪章已经用了一百三十多年。最初是五个单位的议会批准，没有全体居民公投。那时有投票资格的，大约只占成年人的四成。今天的人没有参加过那次立宪，有些后来出生，有些后来入籍，有些只是迁到这里生活。
这段来历值得记住，却不能代替对今天的判断。不能说当年的批准不够广泛，今天整部宪章就当然作废；也不能说祖先已经同意了，后人便只须服从。即使当年真有人人同意，同意也发生在当年。眼前这一项限制是否伤害人，承诺给人的权利是否兑现，人能不能实际提出异议，仍要看眼前。
有些东西，不是宪章写下才第一次有。人在没有共同宪法时，也不是任人伤害的东西。把人身、言论、迁徙写进宪章，是让国家承认并保障这些权利，不是国家忽然慷慨地把它们造出来。因此，删掉一行文字，也不能把人本来就有的资格删掉。投票资格之类依靠共同安排才能运行的权利，又有它自己的制度条件；既然已经承诺，就要真实兑现，不能留着名称悄悄掏空，要改变也须公开说明、接受追问。
不过，不能随便伤害人，是不是意味着应当把某些条文永远锁住？联合城邦后来就有过这样的提案：成员单位不得退出，而且“本条不得修正”。这像是在给未来上一把保险锁。可锁住的究竟是什么？
锁住的是今天这批人写下的这段话，以及以后的人改动它的路。人的尊严不是一句文字能够穷尽的，对它的理解也不应由一个位置永远说了算。可以把底线写进宪章，修改的门槛也可以很高；但文字仍然可以修改，解释仍然可以争论。改了文字，不等于伤害人就变得正当；保护人，也不必靠宣布自己的表述永远完整。那份提案后来因未在同一届两院完成表决而失效，下一届删去了“不得修正”一句。其余部分是否站得住，仍须另问。
## 不能一边按住话筒，一边改下一次开口的日期
回到第十四修正案。三条看上去都只是程序：什么时候选，怎样续期，需要多少票。可程序安排的是，人什么时候能让掌权的位置回答。
选举往后推到“战时状态结束”，而议会多数能够挡住战时状态的终止，下一次接受选举检验的日期，就被放进了被检验者自己手里。紧急状态由采取紧急措施的执政院自己续期，则把原先需要别人确认的那一关挪走了。提高法院门槛，又会使某些原本能够导致改正的多数意见，只剩解释而不能改变行动。三处不完全相同，不能笼统说法院从此消失了；但它们都动到了提问的路。
更要紧的是改动发生的时候。五十人以上集会要许可，广播里的公投节目受到涉军审看，反对广告被要求删改。在这些条件下，即使走的是普通修宪程序，也不能说讨论条件与平时一样。
本系列在这里提出一个比“不得用紧急令修宪”更严格的主张：当紧急措施仍在限制集会、言论、通讯，不应表决那些改动问责安排、或让紧急权力摆脱既有确认与续期的修改。名称不重要，叫修宪、授权法还是紧急立法都一样。等限制解除，让人能说、能组织、能反对，再来决定怎样改。
这不是说紧急期间什么都不得表决。依照既有规则确认、续期，仍要进行，否则反而没人确认。并未改动问责安排、有明确期限的应急立法，也不在这项禁限之内。收回紧急权力、恢复或加强独立审查，更不必等。要挡的是一边限制提问，一边改变以后怎样提问的那一步。
为什么不能等事后再审？因为这一回改的，正是以后审它所要使用的东西。等到事后，选举已经在新的日期上，续期已经换了人决定，法院已经要凑八票。对这一次改动最重要的讨论，没有在原来的条件下发生，事后补一场听证，并不能让那次讨论重新来过。
## 检查的人也不能成为终点
读到这里，常有一个反问：如果宪法也要接受追问，那谁来作最后判断？法院吗？谁又来检查法院？是不是得再设一个更高的法院，一直设下去？
不必把所有路都铺成楼梯。需要的是每一个位置，都有一条它自己关不上的路指向它。法院审查法律和命令，制定规则的人可以修改法院未来适用的规则、追究法官的失职；审查者也不能一句“本院已经决定”，便宣布此后一类问题永远不收。有限的位置彼此接住，不在最顶端放一个不可问的人。它不保证争执立即解决，却不能让任何一方永久握住关门的钥匙。
外面的路也可以帮助。邻国、仲裁、国际机制，能独立审查的，就应按它实际能做的事来用，不能预先说它们都没力量。但若改正要求本国放人、举行选举、停止限制，仍须有人在本国落实。落实不能完全听命于正在被问的机关，否则它不行动，所有路都停在它那里。
由这一点可以说明，国内必须有不被那个机关独占的落实途径。本系列进一步主张，在本级保留制定、执行、检查的功能分立和独立的日常审查。这是另一步制度上的主张，不是前一句已经证明了世界只能有某一种三权设计。数的是功能，不是机构牌子的数量。
联合城邦在战时把军队投诉移交防卫署内部稽查，后来又由执政院指定代理监察长，代理两年没有一份公开报告。这些都是必须检查的线索，不能仅凭“同一个部门”或“谁任命”就断定已经被控制。真正要问的是：被检查者能否独自关闭受理，撤换检查者，压住结案，停掉检查继续所需的资源？投诉实际怎样处理，改正实际能不能发生？
所以，百分之五十八点三是一个真实结果，不是一张从此不必解释的凭证。两万六千名没有投票的人仍在那里，反对的单位仍在那里，以后出生、将承受这套规则的人也会来到。表决可以结束这一次表决，不能替他们把以后所有的问都答完。
body_en: The opposition advertisements were not broadcast as submitted. They mentioned military deployments, so the reviewers required changes. Three border districts had no polling stations at all. About twenty-six thousand registered voters could not vote. In the autumn the result was announced: turnout, 41.2 percent; approval, 58.3 percent. The Fourteenth Amendment took effect.

What had passed? No election to the Chamber of Citizens while the state of war continued; an election within six months of its termination. The chamber’s term would be extended, and the First Executive’s term with it. The Executive Council could renew the emergency itself for up to 180 days at a time; ending it required three fifths of the legislature sitting in joint session. Finally, striking down an emergency order required eight of the Final Court’s eleven judges.

This is another episode from our fictional United City-States of Ends. The Executive Council submitted its proposal twelve days after declaring an emergency. An attached legal memorandum explained the route: an emergency order could not postpone an election, so postponement required a constitutional amendment. The council did not simply disregard that prohibition. It sought to change the arrangements around it.

Nor did the First Executive amend the Charter alone. Both chambers voted, and a referendum followed. The prescribed steps were taken. The difficult question is not whether procedures existed. It is what those procedures can and cannot settle.

Three questions are easily collapsed into one. Does the amendment have practical effect? Yes: elections are delayed and powers continue. Did it take effect under the authority and procedure then in place? In this case file, yes. Is it justified in imposing these consequences on people? The first two answers do not supply the third.
## A signature cannot speak for every generation

The UCSE’s Charter is more than 130 years old. Five constituent legislatures originally ratified it, without a referendum of all residents. Only about four in ten adults were eligible to vote at the time. Most people living under it today were not there. They were born afterward, naturalized afterward, or moved there to live.

Its history matters without settling its present standing. A restricted founding electorate does not automatically invalidate every rule now in force. An honorable founding would not make every present restriction just. Even universal agreement would have occurred then. What a rule does to people now still needs an answer: does it violate their basic boundaries, deliver the rights it promises, and remain open to effective challenge? Those are necessary tests, not a complete certificate of justice.

Some rights were not invented when the Charter named them. People without a common constitution were not objects available for mistreatment. Writing protections of bodily freedom, expression, and movement into a constitution gives institutions obligations to recognize and secure them. It does not create the people’s standing from nothing. Deleting the words cannot erase it. Other rights, such as participation in an established electoral system, depend on shared institutional arrangements. Once those rights have been taken on, the state must deliver them rather than retain the name and quietly empty the promise. Changes require public explanation and challenge.

Does that mean certain clauses should be locked forever? Later in the UCSE’s history, a proposal would prohibit member units from leaving and declare that prohibition unamendable. It sounds like insurance against a dangerous future. But it also makes today’s wording binding on every future attempt to reconsider it.

Human dignity is not exhausted by one sentence. Nor should one office become its permanently unquestionable interpreter. A constitution may declare a fundamental protection, and amending its language may require a very high threshold. The wording should still be revisable. Changing the wording does not make violations just; protecting people does not require claiming that our present formulation is complete. The UCSE proposal lapsed when the chambers failed to complete it within one legislative term. A later version dropped the unamendability clause. Whether its remaining provisions were defensible was a separate question.
## Rewriting the right to ask
The Fourteenth Amendment’s three clauses look procedural: when to vote, who renews an emergency, how many judges must agree. But those are also arrangements for making power answer.

If an election waits until the state of war ends, and the parliamentary majority can block that termination, the people facing the next election acquire control over when it happens. Allowing the council that exercises emergency powers to renew them itself removes an independent checkpoint. Raising the court’s voting threshold changes which judicial conclusions can produce correction. These are not identical changes: the court has not vanished merely because its threshold rises. Yet all three alter the routes through which the authors of the amendment can be challenged.

Now consider the conditions of the referendum. Meetings of more than fifty people needed permission. Military content in referendum broadcasts was reviewed. Opposition advertisements were altered. An ordinary amendment procedure conducted under those restrictions does not offer ordinary conditions for public opposition.

Here the series takes a stricter position than merely forbidding amendment by emergency decree. While emergency measures restrict assembly, expression, or communications, changes to accountability arrangements—or changes freeing emergency powers from existing confirmation and renewal—should not be put to a vote. The label makes no difference: constitutional amendment, enabling act, emergency legislation. Lift the restrictions first, then let people argue about how their future opportunities to challenge power should be arranged.

That does not forbid every vote during an emergency. Confirmation and renewal under existing rules must remain possible; otherwise the very check would be disabled. Time-limited emergency legislation that does not alter accountability arrangements falls outside this prohibition. So do changes withdrawing emergency powers or restoring and strengthening independent review. Opening a door need not wait until the emergency is over.

Why not review the amendment afterward? Because afterward arrives under the arrangements just changed. The election is already postponed, renewal already belongs to a different office, the court already needs eight votes. A later hearing cannot recreate the public discussion that should have taken place before the conditions of challenge were rewritten.
## No final guardian
But if the constitution itself remains answerable, who has the last word? The court? Who reviews the court? Must we build another court above it, then another, forever?

Accountability need not be a staircase. What matters is that every office faces a route of challenge it cannot permanently close. Courts review laws and orders; lawmakers can revise future rules and pursue judges’ misconduct; affected people can bring new evidence, raise new questions, criticize, and vote. The relationships return to offices already in the system instead of ending in an untouchable guardian. This does not promise an immediate solution to every deadlock. It rules out awarding any office a permanent key to shut out its questioners.

External routes can matter as well. Arbitration and international mechanisms should be assessed by what they can actually do, not dismissed in advance as powerless. Still, where a remedy requires this country to release a person, hold an election, or withdraw a restriction, someone within the country must act. If implementation remains entirely at the discretion of the office under challenge, that office’s refusal can stop the remedy.

That establishes the need for domestic implementation beyond that office’s sole control. The series also advocates distinct rule-making, executive, and reviewing functions, including independent domestic day-to-day review. That is an additional institutional commitment, not something the implementation argument has proved to be the world’s only possible constitutional design. Functions matter more than the number of buildings or official titles.

In wartime the UCSE transfers military complaints to an internal audit division of the Office of Defense. Later the Executive Council appoints an acting Inspector General; no public report appears during two years in office. Both are reasons to investigate, not automatic proof of capture. Sharing a department or having been appointed by an executive is not the decisive fact. Can the office being reviewed close intake, remove the reviewer, suppress findings, or cut off the resources needed to continue? What happens to actual complaints and actual corrections?

The referendum’s 58.3 percent is a real result. It is not an exemption from explanation. The twenty-six thousand unable to vote are still there. So are the opposing member units. Others will be born into these arrangements. A vote can finish that vote without answering every question those people will have.
